title: the ranges ahead
hook: three friends photograph the same peak from three valleys and argue over whether it's one mountain
carry: ask what their valley looks like

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and a hymn that ends or perhaps not. Your line was let it be a good question. Did you let one question stay open instead of rushing it shut? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

Three friends go hiking on the same weekend, in three different valleys, and each one posts a photo of the big peak. In the first, it's a sharp tooth of rock. In the second, a long white shoulder. In the third, two summits side by side. The comments fill up. That can't be the same mountain. It is, though. Same rock, same snow, three valleys. Each photo is true, and none of them is the whole thing. Next year, the path spends weeks in a range like that. Today, another of the ranges ahead: the schools of thought, and a Rig Veda line about one truth seen from many valleys.
screen: `ONE PEAK, THREE VALLEYS.` → `EACH PHOTO TRUE.` → `NONE OF THEM THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: The schools are called darshanas, and darshana is a word for seeing. It's the same word people use when they go to a temple for darshan, to see the deity and, some say, to be seen. So a darshana is a way of seeing, a view. Next year the path takes them one at a time. Nyaya, which asks how we know anything at all. Vaisheshika, which looks for the smallest parts of things. Samkhya, which sets awareness beside matter. Yoga, which you've met, the stilling of the mind. Mimamsa, which finds meaning in ritual. And Vedanta, which asks about Brahman and the Self. The promise of the outline is plain: each one is a lens for a week, and none of them is ranked. That doesn't mean the schools agreed. Their teachers argued, sometimes sharply, in long commentaries, and the path will let them argue. And there's a much older line, in the Rig Veda, that fits that valley-by-valley way of looking. In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; the One that is, the sages call by many names. The Sanskrit is short enough to keep: ekam sat, the one that is, and bahudha vadanti, they speak of it in many ways. Readers hear that verse differently. Some hear it about the gods of the hymns, one reality behind many names. Some hear it more widely. Either way, it gives the coming year a shape: many valleys, many photos, and a mountain no single photo holds.
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `ONE SCHOOL A WEEK, NONE RANKED.` · `THE SCHOOLS ARGUED.` · `THE ONE THAT IS, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.` · then, large: `MANY VALLEYS, ONE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one thing, seen more than one way. Choose something near you, a cup, a plant, your own hand. Look at it for a few breaths. Then close the eyes and know it another way: the sounds around it, its weight, the warmth or coolness you remember. Then think of where it came from, and who touched it before you. Same thing, three views, and none of them the whole. If you pray, you can let one of the names you use for God rest in the mind while you sit. If you don't, stay with the thing in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Darshana. A way of seeing: the word for each school of thought ahead, Nyaya, Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta and the rest, taken one valley at a time.
Your line: ask what their valley looks like. Today, when someone sees a thing differently from you, ask what their valley looks like before you say what yours does. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Hindu thought is taught through distinct schools, the darshanas, each with its own root texts and commentaries, and some students learn several of them side by side.

original.note: Sanskrit: darshana, seeing, a view. The word for the schools of thought, and the same word as darshan at a temple.

notes: Day 5 of 'the ranges ahead' (1054–1059). Angle: the darshanas as year four's range, framed by Rig Veda 1.164.46. Days 1054–1056 were not on disk when this was written; check for overlap.

Editor pass: hook's 'the old Hindu habit of looking at one truth from many valleys' (sweeping claim) now points to the Rig Veda line itself; 'many say' to be seen at darshan softened to 'some say'; screen 'the schools argued, and still do' cut to 'the schools argued' (the voice doesn't claim the present); howItsDone 'has long been' and 'often' softened.

Audit (2026-10-01): 'a line in the Rig Veda that sits behind that whole valley-by-valley way of looking' implied RV 1.164.46 underlies the darshanas (unsourced historical claim); now 'a much older line ... that fits' that way of looking. Darshana and temple darshan are the same word (darśana), not 'close to' it; fixed in teach, myth reveal and original note.
The count of the schools is not stated in the voice (the outline says six); the six named follow the outline. One-line descriptions of each school are deliberately simple; confirm they are fair.
Darshana glossed as 'seeing, a view' and linked to temple darshan; this is a meaning, not a stated etymology (both from the root dṛś). Confirm wording.
'Many say' to be seen by the deity at darshan: confirm phrasing is fair.

Rig Veda 1.164.46 paraphrased (indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur ... ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti). The verse also names the heavenly bird Garutman and Yama and Matarishvan; those were left out of the paraphrase for length. Two readings given without ranking.
